title: Why You Can't Save Money (It's Not Your Fault... Mostly)
sources: Federal Reserve Board, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (SHED, May 13, 2026): 63% would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent; 55% have emergency savings covering three months of expenses (59% in 2021)

Federal Reserve SHED 2025, Credit section: 16% of adults used buy now, pay later in the prior 12 months (10% in 2021); slightly more than one in four BNPL users paid late; one in five BNPL users used it for groceries or food delivery
BEA, Personal Income and Outlays, July 2026 (Aug 26, 2026): personal saving rate 3.0% (June 2026: 2.7%)
BEA / FRED PSAVERT: personal saving rate averaged roughly 10%+ in the 1970s (peak 17.3% in May 1975)
IAB/PwC Internet Advertising Revenue Report, Full Year 2025 (Apr 16, 2026): U.S. internet ad revenue $294.6B; social media $117.7B. Per person: $294.6B ÷ ~342M U.S. residents ≈ $860
FTC Staff Report, Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (Sept 2022): fake countdown timers, false scarcity, pre-checked boxes, confirmshaming, hard-to-cancel flows
FTC / ICPEN / GPEN review (July 2024): 76% of 642 subscription websites and apps used at least one dark pattern; nearly 67% used more than one
Amazon 1-Click patent US 5,960,411 (granted Sept 1999, expired Sept 2017)
Madrian & Shea (2001), The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation, Quarterly Journal of Economics: automatic enrollment raised participation from 37% to 86% among new hires
Present bias / hyperbolic discounting: Laibson (1997), Thaler & Benartzi 'Save More Tomorrow' (2004)
Callback: ep10 'Pay in 4, 0% Interest? How Klarna Still Makes Billions' (merchants pay the fee because shoppers spend more)

beats.text: Monday morning. Dave makes a promise. This month, he's saving two hundred dollars. For real this time.
Monday night, his phone buzzes. Flash sale. Forty percent off. Ends in two hours.
One tap. Saved card. Bought. By Friday, Dave has three new packages. And zero dollars saved.
Sound familiar? Here's the thing. That wasn't an accident. That phone was designed to make Dave spend.
Teams of very smart people get paid to remove every tiny moment where you might stop and think.
Today: the one tap store, the pay later button, the ads that follow you, the tricks, your brain, and how Dave finally saves.
First, let's be clear. If saving feels hard, you're in very big company.
The Federal Reserve asks Americans every year: if a surprise four hundred dollar bill showed up, could you pay it with cash?
Only sixty three percent said yes. So more than one in three adults would have to borrow, sell something, or just couldn't pay.
And only fifty five percent have enough emergency savings to cover three months of expenses.
Now look at the whole country. In July, Americans saved just three percent of their income after taxes. Back in the nineteen seventies, it was often above ten percent.
So did everyone suddenly lose their willpower? Or did something change around us? Let's find out.
Imagine a normal store. You walk in. You find the thing. You carry it to the checkout. You wait in line.
You pull out your wallet. You look at the cash. And for one second, your brain asks: do I really need this?
That one second is called friction. And friction is your savings account's best friend.
Online stores figured this out a long time ago. In nineteen ninety nine, Amazon got a patent on buying with just one click.
Today, almost every app does it. Your card is saved. Your address is saved. Your face unlocks the payment. No wallet. No line. No second to think.
It's like a store with a slide that goes straight from the front door to the cash register. Wheee! That will be sixty dollars.
And if the price still makes you pause, there's one more button.
Pay in four. Just fifteen dollars today. Remember our Klarna video?
The store happily pays the pay later company a fee. Why? Because when a price looks smaller, people buy more. And they buy bigger.
According to the Federal Reserve, sixteen percent of American adults used buy now, pay later in the past year. Up from ten percent in twenty twenty one.
More than one in four of those users paid late. And one in five used it for groceries or food delivery.
Four small payments feel like no payment at all. Until they all show up in the same week. Our raccoon loves that week.
Now, how does the store find Dave in the first place? Easy. It lives in his pocket.
Shopping apps send notifications. Price drop! Back in stock! You left something in your cart!
And they often arrive at the perfect moment. At night. On payday. When you're bored on the couch.
Then there's social media. Every scroll, every like, every pause on a video teaches the app what you want.
In twenty twenty five, companies spent about two hundred ninety five billion dollars on internet ads in America. That's roughly eight hundred sixty dollars for every person in the country.
Nobody spends that kind of money unless it works. You are not the customer of those free apps. Your attention is the product.
And some designs go further. They don't just make buying easy. They trick you.
The Federal Trade Commission has a name for them. Dark patterns.
A countdown timer that resets when you refresh the page. Only two left in stock, when there are plenty. A box that's already checked for you.
Or a button that says: no thanks, I don't like saving money. That one is called confirm shaming. Yes, really.
In twenty twenty four, the F T C and regulators from around the world checked six hundred forty two subscription websites and apps. About three out of four used at least one dark pattern.
So when you feel rushed while shopping online, that feeling was often designed. On purpose.
But the tricks only work because of how our brains are built.
Quick test. Would you rather have one hundred dollars today, or one hundred ten dollars next week? Most people grab the hundred today.
Now, one hundred dollars in a year, or one hundred ten in a year and a week? Suddenly, most people say: sure, I'll wait.
Same one week wait. Different answer. Economists call this present bias. Our brains give a huge bonus to anything we can have right now.
It's like there are two Daves. Today Dave wants the sneakers. Future Dave needs the emergency fund. And Today Dave always holds the phone.
Shopping apps are built to talk to Today Dave. Future Dave doesn't even get a vote.
So who profits? Stores sell more. Pay later companies collect fees. And the ad platforms get paid for every click.
And the advice you hear most? Just have more willpower. Stop buying stuff. Most people think that's the whole answer. Nope.
One person's willpower against thousands of engineers and billions of dollars in ads is not a fair fight.
Here's proof that design beats willpower. In a famous study, one company changed its retirement plan so new workers were signed up automatically, unless they chose to leave.
Before the change, about thirty seven percent of new workers joined. After the change? Eighty six percent. Same people. Same paychecks. Just a different default.
So here's the good news. If design can make you spend, design can also make you save. You just have to design it for yourself.
So what can Dave do? Education, not advice.
One. Save first, automatically. Set up a transfer that moves money to savings on payday. Before Dave even sees it, it's gone.
Two. Put savings somewhere a little annoying to reach. A separate account, maybe at a different bank, with no card and no app on the home screen.
Three. Add friction back. Delete saved cards from shopping sites. Log out. Make yourself type the card number every single time.
Four. Delete the shopping apps, or at least turn off their notifications. No buzz, no flash sale.
And five. Use a waiting list. See something you want? Put it on a list and wait two days. Often, the want just melts away.
A few weeks later, Dave checks his savings account. Two hundred dollars. The first time ever. He didn't get more willpower. He just changed the design.
So let's recap.
One. One tap buying, saved cards and pay later buttons remove the second where you'd stop and think.
Two. Notifications, targeted ads, dark patterns and present bias all push you to spend now.
Three. Willpower alone rarely wins. Automate your saving and add friction to your spending.
Next time, Dave's savings finally grow. So he wants to spend them on a shiny new car. Why does buying a new car make you poorer?
